newsitem.title: USA: Disheartened GFOA turns to US Senate on tax plan.
newsitem.headline: Disheartened GFOA turns to US Senate on tax plan.

text.p: Disheartened by muni bond features of U.S. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer's tax package, state and local finance officers are turning to the Senate for help, a spokeswoman said Tuesday.

Catherine Spain, head of the Government Finance Officers Association federal liaison center, said her group will write to roughly 700 state and local government officials urging them to contact their senators."
"We are in the process of putting out a legislative alert to all of our members to try to get them to contact their senators on two (issues)," Spain said.
For one, GFOA opposes Archer's call for extensive repeal of the "de minimis" rule on corporate holdings of tax-exempt bonds, Spain said.
Also, GFOA is deeply disappointed that two arbitrage rebate relief provisions actively sought by the group were not included in the $85 billion plan announced by Archer on Monday.

One provision would have established a safe harbor from U.S. arbitrage rebate rules for bond issuers that reasonably expect to spend 15 percent of bond proceeds within 12 months and 95 percent within three years of the issuance date, Spain said.
The other would have increased the rebate exemption for small issuers from those who reasonably expect to sell only $5 million of tax-exempt bonds in a year to $25 million.

The Ways and Means Committee is scheduled to take up Archer's bill on Wednesday. The Senate, meanwhile, is likely to start work on a tax bill on June 16, Spain said. "They could end their work as soon as June 20," she added.
"Everything is moving so fast," Spain said. "I think we have to go to the Senate.
Regarding de minimis, Archer called for a reduction in allowable de minimis holdings from two percent of a firm's assets to $1 million.
"By taking it down to $1 million, you basically cut out virtually everybody that has an interest in it," Spain said. "You are talking about really small corporations.
